GEO-ANGLE-01.remember: Straight line 180°, around a point 360°, triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, vertically opposite angles equal.
GEO-ANGLE-01.link: Olympiad questions often ask for a sum of many marked angles. Group them into closed shapes before solving individual angles.
GEO-ANGLE-01.why: Angle sums are global constraints. When the requested expression already contains every angle from several triangles or straight lines, adding the closures makes intermediate variables cancel.
GEO-ANGLE-01.notice: Many marked angles; repeated straight lines; the question asks for a total rather than each angle.
GEO-ANGLE-01.try: Circle the smallest closed shapes whose complete angle sets appear in the target. Add those totals first.
GEO-ANGLE-01.contrast: Do not invent equality because two angles look similar. A sketch is not a hypothesis.
GEO-ANGLE-01.example: If six marked angles are exactly the angles of two triangles, their total is 360° without finding any one angle.

GEO-PAR-01.remember: Parallel lines give corresponding and alternate angle equalities. Conversely, the right angle equality can prove lines parallel.
GEO-PAR-01.link: In parallelogram and angle-bisector problems, a half-angle often repeats across the figure because of parallel sides.
GEO-PAR-01.why: Parallelism fixes line directions, so an angle measured from one transversal can be transferred to another location without changing its size.
GEO-PAR-01.notice: Parallel arrows, a parallelogram, or a target asking you to prove lines parallel.
GEO-PAR-01.try: Write one half-angle variable only after marking which angles are guaranteed equal by the parallels.
GEO-PAR-01.contrast: “They look parallel” is never enough. State the theorem direction you are using.
GEO-PAR-01.example: If AB∥CD and a transversal makes 37° with AB, the corresponding acute angle with CD is also 37°.

GEO-POLY-01.remember: For a regular n-gon: exterior turn = 360°/n; interior angle = 180° - 360°/n.
GEO-POLY-01.link: Extended side-line problems are about directions. Undirected lines repeat after 180°, not 360°.
GEO-POLY-01.why: Walking around a regular polygon accumulates equal turns to one full 360° rotation. Side-line directions therefore form an arithmetic progression modulo 180°.
GEO-POLY-01.notice: Regular polygon + extended sides/diagonals + angle between lines.
GEO-POLY-01.try: Let the exterior turn be t=360°/n. Express the line-direction difference as k t modulo 180°.
GEO-POLY-01.contrast: Do not use a giant interior-angle sum when only one line direction is needed.
GEO-POLY-01.example: For a regular octagon, t=45°. Two adjacent side-lines differ by 45° as lines.

GEO-ISO-01.remember: Equal sides give equal opposite angles. An equilateral triangle gives three 60° angles.
GEO-ISO-01.link: Equal-length conditions are often meant to become angle information immediately.
GEO-ISO-01.why: The base-angle theorem converts metric data into angular data, which can then combine with straight lines, right angles, or cyclic angles.
GEO-ISO-01.notice: Two equal segments, repeated equal cuts, or an equilateral construction.
GEO-ISO-01.try: Mark the isosceles triangle and its equal base angles before writing any formula.
GEO-ISO-01.contrast: Do not carry equal lengths as unused metric facts while doing a long angle chase.
GEO-ISO-01.example: If AB=AC and ∠A=74°, then the base angles are each 53°.

GEO-CONG-01.remember: Valid criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS, RHS. Match vertices in the same order.
GEO-CONG-01.link: Sometimes the triangles you ultimately want are not the first pair to prove congruent. A larger pair can reveal the missing equal angles.
GEO-CONG-01.why: Congruence is a legal way to transfer every corresponding side and angle once one accepted criterion is established.
GEO-CONG-01.notice: Crossed equal sides, shared side, right triangles, or a request to prove equal lengths/angles.
GEO-CONG-01.try: Write the candidate correspondence, then list exactly which criterion facts you have.
GEO-CONG-01.contrast: For SAS the known angle must be the included angle between the two known sides.
GEO-CONG-01.example: If AB=DE, AC=DF, and ∠A=∠D, then △ABC and △DEF are congruent by SAS only when those are the included angles.

GEO-TRANS-01.remember: Reflection preserves distances and angles. A 180° rotation about a midpoint swaps the segment endpoints.
GEO-TRANS-01.link: Use a transformation when it manufactures a standard angle or equality that is not visible in the original picture.
GEO-TRANS-01.why: A transformation creates a second copy of the geometry with guaranteed equal lengths/angles, letting a hidden equilateral, isosceles, or symmetric configuration appear.
GEO-TRANS-01.notice: Midpoint symmetry, a stubborn 60°/90° difference, or equal distances to a line through a midpoint.
GEO-TRANS-01.try: Name what the transformation must create before drawing it.
GEO-TRANS-01.contrast: Do not reflect because the picture “looks symmetric”; say which equality the reflection will produce.
GEO-TRANS-01.example: A half-turn about midpoint M sends A to B and any line through M to itself, so perpendicular distances from A and B to that line are equal.

GEO-SIM-01.remember: Similarity criteria: AA, SAS, SSS. A mid-segment is parallel to the third side and half its length. Areas scale as the square of the length scale.
GEO-SIM-01.link: Similarity is useful only after the correspondence is proved. In many area problems, same-base or same-altitude ratios are even shorter.
GEO-SIM-01.why: Parallel lines and equal angles make triangles share shape, so all corresponding lengths scale by one factor.
GEO-SIM-01.notice: Parallel segment inside a triangle, repeated angles, or ratios of cuts from intersecting lines.
GEO-SIM-01.try: Write the triangles in matching order and prove AA before writing a proportion.
GEO-SIM-01.contrast: Do not use a ratio merely because the picture contains two triangles.
GEO-SIM-01.example: A line through the midpoint of AB parallel to BC meets AC at E; then E is the midpoint of AC and DE=BC/2.

GEO-PGRAM-01.remember: A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if opposite sides are both parallel, both equal, one pair is equal and parallel, or diagonals bisect each other.
GEO-PGRAM-01.link: If diagonals also meet at right angles, a parallelogram is a rhombus.
GEO-PGRAM-01.why: Diagonal bisection creates pairs of congruent triangles, forcing opposite sides to match.
GEO-PGRAM-01.notice: Bisecting diagonals, repeated parallelogram constructions, or a target of opposite sides parallel/equal.
GEO-PGRAM-01.try: Check whether a one-line parallelogram test finishes the structure before angle chasing.
GEO-PGRAM-01.contrast: Perpendicular diagonals alone do not imply a rhombus; bisection is the missing condition.
GEO-PGRAM-01.example: If AC and BD bisect each other at O, then ABCD is a parallelogram.

GEO-AREA-01.remember: Triangle area = 1/2 bh. Same altitude -> area ratio = base ratio. Same base -> area ratio = height ratio.
GEO-AREA-01.link: When a rectangle/polygon is cut into pieces, solve for the whole area T before solving every cut length.
GEO-AREA-01.why: Corner triangle areas give products such as height × horizontal cut. Eliminating the cuts can leave one equation only in the total area.
GEO-AREA-01.notice: Several known sub-areas and one unknown central region.
GEO-AREA-01.try: Name the total area T and express each known piece as a product involving a side or cut.
GEO-AREA-01.contrast: Reject algebraic roots that make the whole smaller than the sum of known disjoint pieces.
GEO-AREA-01.example: If three disjoint pieces total 42, no algebraic root T<42 can represent the whole figure.

GEO-TRI-01.remember: For sides a≤b≤c, require a+b>c. Then compare c² with a²+b² for acute/right/obtuse.
GEO-TRI-01.link: Feasibility should be checked before Pythagoras, coordinates, or optimization.
GEO-TRI-01.why: A proposed metric solution is meaningless if the side lengths do not form a non-degenerate triangle.
GEO-TRI-01.notice: Integer sides, a variable third side, or a “for every chosen triple” condition.
GEO-TRI-01.try: Sort the sides and test the largest side against the other two.
GEO-TRI-01.contrast: Triangle inequalities are strict; equality gives a flat triangle.
